overview.summary: Actuaries use mathematics, statistics and financial theory to measure risk and uncertainty, especially in insurance, pensions and investment.
overview.problems: They help organizations price insurance fairly, plan to pay future claims and pensions, and understand financial risk.
overview.worksWith: Insurance and pension managers, underwriters, data analysts, accountants, lawyers and regulators.
overview.workplaces: Insurance companies, consultancies, pension funds, banks and government bodies, mostly in offices.

timeline.title: Plan the day
timeline.description: The actuary reviews deadlines for reports and studies.
timeline.why: Many actuarial reports have legal deadlines.

timeline.title: Gathering and checking data
timeline.description: The actuary collects claims and population data and checks its quality.

timeline.title: Building and testing models
timeline.description: The actuary builds models that estimate future claims, costs or life expectancy, and tests them.
timeline.why: Models guide pricing and how much money is set aside.

timeline.title: Checking assumptions
timeline.description: The actuary asks what happens if assumptions change and writes down the uncertainties.
timeline.why: The future is uncertain, so ranges matter more than single numbers.

timeline.title: Explaining results
timeline.description: The actuary turns the numbers into plain language for managers and clients.
timeline.why: Decision makers need results they can understand.

timeline.title: Exam study
timeline.description: Many actuaries study for professional exams while working.
timeline.why: Qualifications are required to progress in the profession.

responsibilities: Analyzing data on risk and uncertainty
Building and testing financial and statistical models
Pricing insurance and setting aside money for future claims
Advising on pensions and investment risk
challenges: Professional exams are demanding and take years.
The work involves heavy mathematical and spreadsheet work.
Results are uncertain, and explaining uncertainty to non-experts is hard.
Much of the day is spent sitting at a computer.
There are fewer roles than in some careers, so competition can be strong.
workEnvironment: Mostly offices or remote work with computers and spreadsheets, working with teams and managers. Hours are usually regular, with study time for exams. Work follows reporting cycles with busy peaks.
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary by country and firm

activity.title: Estimate a simple risk with dice
steps: Choose a simple event, such as getting at least one six when you roll a die four times.
Predict how often it will happen.
Run the experiment 50 times and record each result.
Compare your result with your prediction and calculate the percentage.
Write one sentence on why small experiments can differ from the theory.
activity.outcome: You practise estimating probability, running a test and understanding uncertainty.
activity.safety: Use only dice, coins or cards, do not gamble with money, and do not use this to make decisions about real risks.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
